summary: This memo reproduces three letters exchanged between the Internet Activities Board and the Defense Information Systems Agency about using the Domain Name System everywhere on the Internet and phasing out older host name tables. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Instead of everyone keeping a copy of one big name list, computers can ask a shared directory. These letters are two groups agreeing that the shared directory is the better way.

questions: iab and disa letters on dns
phasing out hosts.txt in favor of dns
why dns is better than static host tables
subtitle: Letters on adopting the Domain Name System across the entire Internet

tldr.problem: Parts of the Internet still used static host name tables instead of the dynamic Domain Name System, causing inconsistent information and preventing features like email relay prioritization.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Activities Board wrote to the Defense Information Systems Agency arguing that adopting DNS everywhere would improve network reliability and management, with DISA acknowledging the importance and committing to study the issue.
tldr.outcome: The exchange established DNS adoption as a policy goal and helped motivate the eventual phase-out of host table-based naming.

today: DNS became the universal standard for host name resolution on the Internet. The static hosts.txt file approach is now obsolete. Today, DNS underpins nearly all Internet operations, from web browsing to email delivery to application APIs, and the phase-out that the IAB and DISA discussed in 1992 is complete.

sections.title: The Problem with Static Host Tables
sections.content: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a distributed database that lets computers look up host names and find their IP addresses. However, in the early 1990s, parts of the Internet still used a static file called hosts.txt, a centrally maintained table of all host names and addresses. This approach had major drawbacks: the central file became increasingly outdated, data could not scale with the rapidly growing Internet, and systems using only the static table missed important features that DNS provided, such as Mail eXchange (MX) records that allow mail servers to specify backups and priorities.
sections.eli5: Keeping one giant list and photocopying it to everyone is slow and the copies get out of date. A shared directory that people can ask anytime is much faster and always current.

sections.title: Why DNS is Better
sections.content: The DNS overcomes these problems with a distributed architecture. Instead of maintaining one central file, DNS uses a hierarchy of authoritative servers that can be updated quickly. New hosts added to the Internet register their names in DNS immediately, not by waiting for updates to a central list. DNS also supports features that static tables cannot: MX records let administrators specify mail relay servers and their priorities, making email delivery more resilient. Additionally, DNS queries are dynamic, so the information is always current. By the early 1990s, almost all of the Internet had adopted DNS, but significant fractions (particularly in the MILNET community) still depended on the static hosts.txt approach.
sections.eli5: With DNS, you ask a local expert who can ask bigger experts if needed. With a static file, you check a photocopy that might be weeks old. DNS also lets you say which backup server to use if the main one is down.

sections.title: The IAB's Case for Universal DNS
sections.content: The Internet Activities Board (IAB) wrote to the Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) in March 1992, making a strong case for universal DNS adoption. The IAB argued that mixing naming approaches caused inconsistent and outdated information, leading to connectivity failures. It emphasized that commercial TCP/IP software already supported DNS, so mandating its use would not impose new costs on vendors. The IAB also noted that hosts using only static tables were becoming an obstacle to network operations and management, and that as the rest of the Internet community moved toward DNS, those still using static files were becoming increasingly isolated. The IAB called for policy-level decisions and deadlines for converting all Internet components to uniform DNS use.
sections.eli5: The IAB told DISA that everyone should switch to DNS. They explained that mixing both ways caused problems, that it was already easy to do, and that staying behind was like refusing to upgrade to a phone system everyone else used.

sections.title: DISA's Response and Commitment
sections.content: DISA, which oversees military network standards, responded in April 1992 acknowledging the importance of the DNS issue for both performance and interoperability. DISA committed to studying the technical and economic impacts on Department of Defense systems and promised to inform the IAB of the results. In May 1992, the IAB replied, expressing appreciation for DISA's attention and proposing to arrange a meeting to discuss issues of mutual concern. The exchange, though brief, represented a formal commitment from the DoD's protocol standards body to consider DNS adoption as a serious policy matter rather than a technical detail left to individual system managers.
sections.eli5: DISA agreed it was important and said they would study it. The IAB and DISA agreed to keep talking about it. This was important because the military had its own networks and convinced them to switch helped a lot.
